item.title: Texas oil and gas, July 2026: oil down 11.6% on a year before, gas flat
item.dc:creator: Royalty Clerk
item.description:
The Texas Railroad Commission's newest production file came out in late October. It fills in July 2026 and brings the first reports for August. Here is what it shows, and what it means for a royalty check.

Texas as a whole

In July 2026, 138,490 Texas leases reported 159.5 million barrels of oil and condensate and 1.17 billion mcf of gas.

  • Oil is down 11.6% on July 2025, when it was 180.4 million barrels.
  • Gas is nearly flat, down 0.3% on July 2025.
  • Oil is up 0.9% on June 2026 (158.1 million barrels).

One caution: operators are still filing late reports for July, so its totals will rise a little and the gap with last year will narrow. July 2025 has had a year to settle. August has 124,633 leases reporting so far, too early to read.

The top ten oil counties

Barrels of oil and condensate in July 2026, against July 2025:

  • Martin County: 20.37 million barrels (down 6.2%)
  • Midland County: 19.61 million barrels (down 6.0%)
  • Reeves County: 13.63 million barrels (down 11.8%)
  • Loving County: 13.34 million barrels (down 13.7%)
  • Upton County: 9.12 million barrels (up 0.4%)
  • Reagan County: 6.93 million barrels (up 9.1%)
  • Karnes County: 5.86 million barrels (down 36.5%)
  • Howard County: 5.65 million barrels (down 35.2%)
  • Andrews County: 5.40 million barrels (down 11.6%)
  • Ward County: 4.84 million barrels (down 4.6%)

Karnes and Howard stand out, both down by more than a third. That can come from late reports, fewer new wells coming on, or older wells declining. It does not mean anyone's royalty is wrong, but if your lease is in one of those counties, look at your own lease's numbers.

What it means for your check

Texas law gives operators 60 days after the end of the month oil is sold to pay for it, and 90 days for gas. So the checks arriving now mostly pay for July and August production. A check is roughly volume times price, less taxes and any deductions your lease allows. If yours dropped, the first question is whether your lease produced less, or whether the price or the deductions changed.

You can see your own lease's monthly volumes back to 1993 with Look up a lease, and compare them with your check stub using Why is my royalty check lower?. The Texas oil and gas atlas covers every county.

Next issue: when the Railroad Commission posts its next file at the end of November, with August filled in.

item.title: Operator changes, July 2026: 1,850 Texas leases got a new operator
item.dc:creator: Royalty Clerk
item.description:
In July 2026, 1,850 Texas leases were first reported under a new operator, in 69 moves between operators. Sixty companies gained leases.

The biggest moves

  • Diversified Production LLC to Eagleridge Operating, LLC: 1,139 leases
  • Jay Management Company, LLC to Great American Resources Inc.: 214 leases
  • 84 Energy LLC to Iron Jaw Operating LLC: 112 leases
  • Overton Park Oil & Gas LP to Hilcorp Energy Company: 48 leases
  • Roy Jackson Energy Operating to Lakeshore Operating, LLC: 41 leases
  • Eagle Oil & Gas Co. to Fortune Resources LLC: 38 leases
  • Walsh & Watts, Inc. to United Oil & Shale LLC: 27 leases
  • Durango Resources Corp. to Aransas Operating Company, LLC: 25 leases

July was not unusual. Between January and July 2026, 15,796 Texas leases changed operators, with the biggest months in January (4,291) and May (6,167). August shows 589 so far, but its reports are still coming in.

Why a new operator matters to an owner

The operator is usually the company that pays your royalty. When a lease is sold, the old company stops paying and the new one has to set you up from scratch: your name, address, decimal interest and tax ID. The months on either side of the switch are when a payment is most often missed.

What to watch for:

  • A letter or a new division order from the new company. Check that the decimal matches your old check stubs before you sign. Under Texas law a division order does not amend your lease.
  • A gap of a month or two is common. If it runs longer, write to the new operator and include the owner number from your old stub.
  • Money held in suspense while the paperwork catches up still belongs to you, and Texas law adds interest to late royalty payments.

The Texas operator changes page lists every change from the last 24 months. If your checks have already stopped, start with If your royalty checks stopped. If the company on your old stub no longer exists, find who took it over.

item.title: Where Texas gas went in July 2026: 0.81% flared, up from 0.73% a year before
item.dc:creator: Royalty Clerk
item.description:
Every month, each Texas operator reports where its lease's gas went. In July 2026, Texas leases reported moving 1.17 billion mcf of gas:

  • 49.9% to a processing plant
  • 46.6% to a transmission line
  • 2.3% burned as lease fuel
  • 0.81% (9.5 million mcf) vented or flared
  • the last 0.4% to other uses, such as gas lift and repressuring

The flared share was 0.73% in July 2025. This year it jumped to 1.26% in April and has come down since.

Where flaring changed most

Counties with the biggest change in flared gas, July 2026 against July 2025 (mcf flared, then the share of the county's gas):

  • Upton County: 902,044 mcf, 2.10% of its gas, up from 0.87%
  • Reagan County: 656,649 mcf, 1.27% of its gas, up from 0.73%
  • Winkler County: 416,560 mcf, 6.30% of its gas, up from 1.90%
  • Howard County: 979,496 mcf, 2.88% of its gas, up from 1.96%
  • Martin County: 588,511 mcf, 0.84% of its gas, down from 1.22%
  • Yoakum County: 445,644 mcf, 7.89% of its gas, up from 4.59%
  • Pecos County: 204,287 mcf, 2.35% of its gas, up from 0.57%
  • Ward County: 409,462 mcf, 2.13% of its gas, down from 3.10%

Reeves County flared the most gas of any county, 1.02 million mcf, but that is only 1.01% of its gas, up from 0.84%.

Why it matters for a royalty

Most Texas leases pay royalty on gas that is sold. Gas that is flared or burned on the lease is not sold, so it usually earns the owner nothing. If your lease's flared share jumps from one month to the next, it is fair to ask the operator why: a pipeline outage, a full plant, or a well not yet connected.

A switch between the plant code and the pipeline code can also change your statement, bringing plant products and processing fees onto it. What the disposition codes mean explains each code, and every lease page on Royalty Clerk shows its own gas month by month. If your check fell, Why is my royalty check lower? walks through the usual causes.

item.title: Texas drilling permits, September 2026: 682 new wells, most in Martin County
item.dc:creator: Royalty Clerk
item.description:
The Railroad Commission issued 761 drilling permits in September 2026. 682 were for new wells, up 14.8% on August (594). 590 of the new wells, or 86.5%, are horizontal. The other permits were for recompletions (63), re-entries (11) and smaller changes.

New-well permits have stayed in a narrow band all year: 660 in April, 652 in May, 684 in June, 611 in July, 594 in August and 682 in September. October stood at 656 as of October 30.

Counties with the most new-well permits

  • Martin County: 103 new wells, 102 horizontal
  • Loving County: 59 new wells, all horizontal
  • Midland County: 44 new wells, all horizontal
  • Reagan County: 41 new wells, all horizontal
  • Webb County: 29 new wells, all horizontal
  • Upton County: 24 new wells, all horizontal
  • Reeves County: 22 new wells, 18 horizontal
  • Dimmit County: 22 new wells, all horizontal
  • Winkler County: 19 new wells, 14 horizontal
  • Karnes County: 15 new wells, all horizontal
  • McMullen County: 15 new wells, all horizontal
  • Crane County: 14 new wells, all horizontal

Operators with the most new-well permits

  • Pioneer Natural Res. USA, Inc.: 67
  • Diamondback E&P LLC: 53
  • De Central Operating, LLC: 32
  • Silver Hill Energy Operating LLC: 23
  • Anadarko E&P Onshore LLC: 20
  • Apache Corporation: 15
  • Oxyrock Operating, LLC: 14
  • EOG Resources, Inc.: 14

What a permit near you means

A permit is the first public sign of a new well. Drilling, completion and first sales come later, often many months later, and not every permit gets drilled. If a new well does produce from your minerals, expect a division order from the operator. Under Texas law, the first payment is due within 120 days after the end of the month of first sale.

Texas well watch lists new permits county by county, so you can see what is planned near your land.

item.title: What 6.8 million Texas mineral accounts can tell an heir
item.dc:creator: Royalty Clerk
item.description:
Texas counties tax producing mineral interests like any other property. Each county's appraisal district keeps a roll with an account for every interest it taxes, in the owner's name, down to very small fractions of a lease.

We now search more than 140 of those county rolls, holding 6.8 million mineral accounts. About 81% of the accounts match a Railroad Commission lease, which is how we connect a name on a roll to the oil and gas behind it.

The largest rolls

  • Tarrant County, 2026 roll: 1,207,746 accounts
  • Midland County, 2026 roll: 442,391 accounts
  • Panola County, 2026 roll: 400,481 accounts
  • Upton County, 2026 roll: 296,772 accounts
  • Martin County, 2026 roll: 243,324 accounts
  • Howard County, 2026 roll: 236,720 accounts
  • Harrison County, 2026 roll: 214,452 accounts
  • Wise County, 2026 roll: 200,260 accounts
  • Karnes County, 2026 roll: 181,923 accounts
  • Reeves County, 2024 roll: 166,754 accounts

Tarrant's roll is the largest by far because the Barnett Shale runs under Fort Worth and its suburbs, where many homeowners hold a small mineral interest.

Why a roll helps when someone dies

An heir often does not know what a parent owned. The appraisal roll is one of the few public places where a mineral interest appears under a person's name. If a name is on a roll, the county believes that person owns a producing interest, and a tax bill has been going out for it, often to an old address.

  • Search the rolls by name with the mineral interest finder.
  • If a tax bill came for an interest you did not know about, mineral property tax by county explains the bill and how to protest a value.
  • Royalties an operator could not deliver may have gone to the state: see Texas unclaimed royalties.

We publish counts only. No owner's name or address is on any public page.

item.title: 33 years of Texas oil and gas records, 1993 to 2026
item.dc:creator: Royalty Clerk
item.description:
Our Texas production records now reach back to January 1993. They hold every monthly production report in the Railroad Commission's public data, more than 64 million filings across more than 350,000 leases, through August 2026.

Over those 33 years, Texas leases produced 31.6 billion barrels of oil and condensate and 267.4 billion mcf of gas.

The top oil counties since 1993

Barrels of oil and condensate, January 1993 through August 2026:

  • Midland County: 2.35 billion barrels
  • Martin County: 2.01 billion barrels
  • Reeves County: 1.79 billion barrels
  • Karnes County: 1.53 billion barrels
  • Loving County: 1.46 billion barrels
  • Upton County: 1.29 billion barrels
  • Andrews County: 1.18 billion barrels
  • Howard County: 1.16 billion barrels
  • Yoakum County: 959 million barrels
  • De Witt County: 865 million barrels

The shale years show up plainly. In Midland, Martin, Reeves, Loving and Howard counties, more oil came out between January 2020 and August 2026 than in the 27 years before. Midland produced 872 million barrels from 1993 through 2019, and 1.48 billion since. Karnes runs the other way: its Eagle Ford boom came in the 2010s, with 852 million barrels before 2020 and 678 million since.

The top gas counties since 1993

  • Webb County: 17.7 billion mcf
  • Panola County: 12.2 billion mcf
  • Reeves County: 10.7 billion mcf
  • Tarrant County: 9.9 billion mcf
  • Midland County: 7.9 billion mcf
  • Zapata County: 6.8 billion mcf
  • Loving County: 6.1 billion mcf
  • Pecos County: 6.1 billion mcf

Tarrant is the Barnett Shale under Fort Worth. Webb and Zapata sit on the border near Laredo.

Why old records matter to a family

Many people find us after a parent or grandparent dies and a check stub or a tax bill turns up with a lease name on it. With records back to 1993, a lease page shows that lease's whole life: when it started producing, which operators ran it, and whether it still produces today. A lease that still produces is usually still in force, which means someone is still owed royalty on it.

  • Look up a lease by name or Railroad Commission number.
  • Is my oil lease still active? explains how to tell.
  • Inherited mineral rights in Texas covers the first steps for heirs.

The county figures are also free to download as an open dataset: Texas oil and gas production by county, 1993 to 2026.
